lessons.title: Know what a row represents

steps.headline: A row is one thing, and its primary key is its name.

lead.text: A table is a grid. Each row is one thing, such as one order. Each column is one fact about it.
A primary key is a column that differs in every row, so it names the row. In these tables it is id.
A column that holds another table's key, like customer_id, can repeat.
Two tables sit side by side. Each row of each table stands for one thing, and the id column names that thing.

reveal.text: You can read it from the ids: 101 to 106 are order numbers. Ada has one row in customers and two in orders, so a row in orders is an order, not a person.

queries.label: Ids and names
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ids and references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Which items did Ben order?

workedSteps.text: Find Ben in customers.
Pick the rows of orders whose customer_id is 2.
Read the item column of those rows.

queries.label: Ada's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ben's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: orders.customer_id stores the id of the customer who placed each order. To follow a customer, read that column.

reveal.text: You counted by the column's value, not by names. That is how a row in one table points at a row in another.

queries.label: Ada's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ben's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Order 106 was taken by phone and nobody has confirmed its price. The amount cell still has to hold something.

reveal.text: Whichever you chose, the question was what the cell claims. NULL claims nothing about the amount; 0 would claim the order was free.

queries.label: Unknown amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Elm signs up today and has not ordered anything yet. Elm gets a row in one table only.

queries.label: Count customers
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers;

queries.label: Count orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders;

lessons.orientation: Identify the thing each table row represents and keep missing values distinct from zero.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café notebook has one line for each cup sold. On Monday Mia bought 3 cups and Sam bought 2 cups.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what one row stands for, and keep an unknown value apart from zero.

recap.keyIdea: A row stands for one thing and its primary key names it, so count rows by that thing, and record a missing value as NULL, never as 0.

blocks.text: You counted 5 lines for Monday's cups, 2 order rows for customer 1, and 5 customers once Elm joined, and each count followed the thing a row stands for.

recap.nextHook: Now ask a table for only the columns you need.

lessons.title: Choose the columns you need

steps.headline: SELECT chooses the columns of the result, and FROM names the table.

lead.text: A query reads a table and builds a new result. SELECT lists the columns you want in that result. FROM names the table to read.
The stored table never changes. Only the result is shaped.
Two queries read the same orders table. One asks for every column. The other names two columns.

reveal.text: You counted the names in the SELECT list. Both results have the same six rows, but the second is two columns wide.

queries.label: All fields
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Show amount under the heading price.

workedSteps.text: Name the column you want to show.
Add AS and the heading you want.
Put it in the SELECT list.
workedSteps.math: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders;

queries.label: Query A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Query B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A SELECT list can hold an expression. It is worked out once for every row. An unknown amount stays unknown, so NULL stays NULL.

reveal.text: You applied the expression to a row's amount. Every row gets its own result, and the table is not touched.

queries.label: Original amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Double each amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount * 2 AS doubled FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Changing the expression changes the question. The first query scales each amount. This one adds a fixed sum.

queries.label: Multiply by two
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount * 2 AS doubled FROM orders WHERE id = 102;

queries.label: Add ten
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount + 10 AS increased FROM orders WHERE id = 102;

lessons.orientation: Use SELECT and aliases to shape a result without changing the stored table.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: You hide every column of a six-column spreadsheet except three, then send that view to a colleague.

intro.promise: By the end you'll shape a query result with SELECT, AS and simple expressions, knowing the stored table never changes.

recap.keyIdea: SELECT shapes the result with the columns and expressions you list. AS labels them, and the stored table stays exactly as it was.

blocks.text: You counted 2 result columns, then doubled 80 and added 10 to 20. The orders table never changed.

recap.nextHook: Next, keep only the rows that answer your question.

lessons.title: Write the condition you mean

steps.headline: WHERE keeps only the rows whose condition is true.

lead.text: A condition is a test on each row, such as amount > 50. WHERE keeps the rows that pass and drops the rest.
A comparison with an unknown amount is never true, so those rows are dropped too. To find unknown amounts, write IS NULL.
Two queries filter the same orders, with a higher threshold in the second. One amount is unknown.

reveal.text: You tested each amount against the boundary, which counts. The unknown amount dropped out because a comparison with it is never true.

queries.label: At least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: At least 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= 80 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Keep orders that are paid or worth at least 40.

workedSteps.text: Keep every row that passes the first test, status = 'paid'.
Add rows that pass the second test and are not kept yet.
Order 106 is pending and its amount is unknown, so it passes neither test.

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: AND is stricter than OR. A row must pass every test joined by AND.

reveal.text: You kept only rows that passed both tests. Adding a test with AND can only remove rows.

queries.label: Both conditions
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Either condition
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' OR amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Boundaries decide close calls. Compare a range that includes its ends with one that leaves them out.

reveal.text: You decided what happens to an amount exactly on a boundary. BETWEEN keeps it. A strict comparison drops it.

queries.label: Range A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 20 AND 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Range B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 20 AND amount < 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A list of accepted values is another kind of condition. IN ('Book', 'Lamp') keeps a row whose item is either name. An unknown amount does not change an item.

queries.label: Book or Lamp
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item IN ('Book', 'Lamp') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Starts with B
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE item LIKE 'B%' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Missing amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Use SQL conditions to select exactly the rows your question requires.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bookshop sign says 'Books at least £20'. The shelf holds books priced 5, 12, 20, 25 and 30 pounds.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write conditions that keep exactly the rows you mean, including at the boundary and for unknown values.

recap.keyIdea: WHERE keeps the rows whose condition is true. Choose the comparison, the boundary and AND or OR for exactly the rows you mean.

blocks.text: You counted 3 orders of at least 40 and 2 that were paid and large. Unknown amounts passed no comparison.

recap.nextHook: Next, put the rows you kept into a useful order.

lessons.title: Make the first row meaningful

steps.headline: ORDER BY puts rows in a stated order, and LIMIT keeps the first few.

lead.text: Rows have no promised order until you ask. ORDER BY amount DESC puts the largest first, and ASC puts the smallest first. LIMIT 3 then keeps the first three rows of that order.
Without ORDER BY, 'first' means nothing.
The same six orders come back in two different orders. Only one part of a query can promise which order you get.

reveal.text: You picked the part that states an order. Layout and SELECT alone promise nothing, so ask for the order whenever first or last matters.

queries.label: Order A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Order B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

steps.headline: Put the largest known amount first, with higher ids winning ties.

workedSteps.text: Leave out the unknown amount with WHERE amount IS NOT NULL.
Sort by amount, largest first. The two 80s tie.
Add id DESC to settle each tie.

queries.label: Lower id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

lead.text: Compare amounts first. When two rows tie, the next sort column decides.

reveal.text: You settled a tie with the second sort column. That is what makes the first row meaningful.

queries.label: Lower id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Higher id wins ties
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id DESC;

lead.text: LIMIT keeps the first rows of the ordered result. It finds the largest only because the order puts them first.

reveal.text: You ordered first and kept the first rows. A limit with no meaningful order would not find the largest.

queries.label: Top two
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Top three
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 3;

lead.text: WHERE chooses the eligible rows first. Then the order and the limit pick from them.

queries.label: Smallest paid
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount ASC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

queries.label: Largest paid
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC LIMIT 2;

lessons.orientation: Use a deterministic order to decide which rows a limited result retains.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Five runners finish a race in 31, 28, 35, 30 and 29 seconds. Medals go to the three fastest.

intro.promise: By the end you'll order rows so the first one means something, and keep just the top few.

recap.keyIdea: Only ORDER BY promises an order. Add a unique tie-breaker, and LIMIT keeps the first rows of that order.

blocks.text: You kept the first three of the ordered times and settled a tie between two 80s by id. The top three known amounts added up to 200.

recap.nextHook: Next, remove repeats so each answer appears once.

lessons.title: Count distinct things

steps.headline: DISTINCT keeps each different result row once.

lead.text: A result can repeat itself. SELECT DISTINCT removes a row only when it matches another row in every selected column.
DISTINCT changes the result. The stored table keeps every row.
Several orders point at the same customer. One query lists every reference, and the other removes repeats.

reveal.text: Each customer id counted once, no matter how many orders repeat it. The table itself still holds every order.

queries.label: Every reference
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Distinct customers
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

steps.headline: Does DISTINCT item, id remove any rows?

workedSteps.text: Read the whole SELECT list as one row.
Compare pairs, not items alone.
No two pairs match, so every row stays.

queries.label: Distinct items
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item FROM orders ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Distinct item and id
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The amount column holds 80, 20, 80, 40, 20 and NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT amount) counts the different known amounts. NULL is not a known amount.

reveal.text: You counted values rather than orders and skipped the unknown one. Listing distinct values and counting them are different questions.

queries.label: Distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT amount FROM orders ORDER BY amount;

queries.label: Count known distinct amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: DISTINCT works on the whole selected row. This time the row is a customer paired with a status.

queries.label: Item and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT item, status FROM orders ORDER BY item, status;

queries.label: Customer and status
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, status FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, status;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish result rows, distinct values and distinct combinations of values.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bakery's till log for the day reads: bun, loaf, bun, roll, bun, bagel, loaf.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count different values and different combinations, and know what DISTINCT leaves alone.

recap.keyIdea: DISTINCT collapses result rows that match in every selected column. It changes the result only, so choose the columns you want to compare.

blocks.text: You counted 4 kinds of bread, then 3 customer ids and 5 customer and status pairs. Adding a column made more rows count as different.

recap.nextHook: Next, boil many rows down to one summary number.

lessons.title: Choose the right denominator

steps.headline: An aggregate turns many rows into one value, using only the known values.

lead.text: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX on a column use only its known values.
COALESCE(amount, 0) swaps an unknown for 0 before the aggregate sees it. That changes what they see.
The orders table has six rows, and one amount is unknown. Compare counting rows with counting a column.

reveal.text: You left out the unknown amount, so the column count came out one short of the row count. That gap is how a missing value shows.

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

steps.headline: Find the average amount for customer 3's orders.

workedSteps.text: List the amounts for customer 3.
AVG uses only the known amounts.
COALESCE(amount, 0) would count the unknown as 0 instead.

queries.label: Known amounts only
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: Unknown counted as zero
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: SUM adds the known amounts. AVG divides that sum by the number of known amounts.

reveal.text: You divided by the known amounts only. The unknown amount neither adds to the total nor counts as an order.

queries.label: Keep missing separate
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill missing with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

lead.text: MIN and MAX pass over unknown values too. Filter first, then pick from the rows that are left.

reveal.text: You picked from the known amounts of the filtered rows. An unknown amount never stands in for a smallest value.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

lead.text: Suppose WHERE leaves no rows at all. An aggregate query still returns a single row. Think about what a total of nothing means.

queries.label: Known orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matches
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lessons.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX while keeping missing values visible.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three answered 4, 6 and 8. The fourth did not answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know which rows each aggregate counts, and what an unknown value does to a total or an average.

recap.keyIdea: Aggregates use only known values: the denominator is the count of known amounts. COALESCE changes that by filling the gaps first.

blocks.text: You found an average of 6 from three answers and 48 from five known amounts. With no rows, a SUM came back NULL.

recap.nextHook: Next, summarise each group of rows separately.

lessons.title: Build a grouped report

steps.headline: GROUP BY makes each result row stand for a group, and HAVING filters the groups.

lead.text: GROUP BY item gathers orders with the same item. Each group becomes one result row, and SUM works inside the group.
WHERE filters rows before the groups are made. HAVING filters groups after their totals exist.
Several orders share an item. Group them, and the report's rows stand for something new.

reveal.text: You counted the different items. The report now has one row per item instead of one per order.

queries.label: Group by item
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Group by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

steps.headline: Report each status with its orders, known amounts and total.

workedSteps.text: Group the orders by status.
Count rows and known amounts in each group.
Add the known amounts in each group.

queries.label: Counts by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: With totals
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

lead.text: Inside a group, COUNT(amount) counts only that group's known amounts.

reveal.text: You counted inside one group. A grouped report can show both counts, so incomplete groups stand out.

queries.label: Order counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Known amount counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

lead.text: WHERE works on single rows, before any groups exist. A group's total exists only once the groups are made.

reveal.text: You named the clause that tests finished groups. Keep the row filter and the group filter apart in your head.

queries.label: Total at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Total at least 200
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 200 ORDER BY item;

lead.text: Filter the rows first, then group what is left. Read the row filter and the group filter separately.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Paid total at least 50
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 50 ORDER BY item;

lessons.orientation: Build a report whose rows represent groups, then filter its calculated totals.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café keeps slips: tea £2, coffee £3, tea £4, coffee £1 and tea £1.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build a report with one row per group, and filter rows before grouping or groups afterwards.

recap.keyIdea: GROUP BY makes each result row a group. WHERE filters rows before grouping, and HAVING filters the totals afterwards.

blocks.text: You grouped orders into 3 items and counted 1 known Lamp amount. A paid Desk total came to 160.

recap.nextHook: Next, bring two tables together with a join.

lessons.title: Follow a relationship between tables

steps.headline: A join pairs rows whose key values match.

lead.text: Orders store a customer_id, and customers store the name. JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id pairs each order with the customer whose id matches.
An INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that match.
Orders refer to customers by number. Join the two tables on that number, and count the pairs that match.

reveal.text: You counted matching pairs, not names. Each order matched the one customer it refers to, so the rows still stand for orders.

queries.label: Order references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names attached
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

steps.headline: Which customers have placed an order?

workedSteps.text: Join customers to orders on c.id = o.customer_id.
workedSteps.math: one row for each matching pair

workedSteps.text: Look for customers with no pair.
SELECT DISTINCT c.name keeps each matched name once.

queries.label: One row per match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Customers who ordered
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

lead.text: CROSS JOIN has no condition. It pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.

reveal.text: You paired each customer with each order. That is not the same as the orders each customer placed.

queries.label: Match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A join condition should follow the relationship the tables store. A condition that is not that relationship can match nothing, or the wrong rows.

queries.label: Paid matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Wrong columns
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.id ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Join keys deliberately and account for every matching pair.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Each pupil has a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. Club 1 is Chess.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two tables on their key and say how many rows to expect.

recap.keyIdea: An INNER JOIN pairs rows whose keys match, so a row with no match disappears and a row with several matches repeats.

blocks.text: You matched 2 pupils to Chess, then counted 6 matching pairs between customers and orders. A cross join of the same tables gives 24.

recap.nextHook: Next, keep the customers who have no matching order.

lessons.title: Keep the customers with no orders

steps.headline: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, matched or not.

lead.text: JOIN keeps only matches. LEFT JOIN customers ... orders keeps every customer.
If a customer has no order, the order columns are filled with NULL.
That NULL means no order matched. It is not an order with a missing amount.
Six orders match their customers, and one customer has no order. Join the tables so that every customer stays.

reveal.text: You kept every match and added the customer with none. The unmatched row is still a row of the result.

queries.label: Only matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Keep every customer
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

steps.headline: Count Cy's rows, orders and known amounts after the LEFT JOIN.

workedSteps.text: Cy matched two orders, so the join gives two rows.
Count an order column that is always filled on a match.
One matched order has no amount, and COUNT(o.amount) skips it.

queries.label: Cy's rows, orders and known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, COUNT(o.amount) AS known_amounts FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id = 3 GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

queries.label: Cy's joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id = 3 ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: COUNT of a column ignores NULL. After a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no match has NULL in every order column.

reveal.text: You counted matched orders, not rows. Counting a column from the right table gives zero for a customer with none.

queries.label: Count joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: In Dee's row every orders column is NULL. A test written after the join runs on those NULLs.

reveal.text: You decided where the paid test belongs. A test in ON limits which orders match. A test in WHERE can remove the preserved customer.

queries.label: Version one
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Version two
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: To find customers with no order, test a column from orders. Think about which columns can be NULL on a real order.

queries.label: No matching order
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No known amount
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.amount IS NULL ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

recap.nextHook: Next, keep the unmatched rows from both sides.

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows on either side

steps.headline: RIGHT JOIN keeps every right row, and FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both sides.

lead.text: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table. RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table.
FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both. Wherever one side has no match, its columns are NULL.
Orders now include a guest order, 107, with no customer. Dee still has no order. Each join preserves one side.

reveal.text: You picked the side that RIGHT keeps: the table written on the right. Its unmatched row stays, and the other side's unmatched row is dropped.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

steps.headline: List every customer and every order, matched or not.

workedSteps.text: Keep every matched pair.
workedSteps.math: Ada 101, Ada 102, Ben 103, Ben 104, Cy 105, Cy 106

workedSteps.text: Keep the customer who matches no order.
Keep the order that matches no customer.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve both sides
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the matched pairs and the unmatched rows from both sides.

reveal.text: You added the matches to the unmatched rows from each side. Both kinds of absence are rows of the result.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve both sides
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: After a full join, a NULL key shows which side had no match.

reveal.text: You read the NULL key to see which side was absent. A row count alone cannot tell you that.

queries.label: First test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Second test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: A condition in ON decides which rows can pair. Rows that fail it are still kept as unmatched rows.

queries.label: Match every status
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Only paid matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

recap.nextHook: Next, use one query's answer inside another.

lessons.title: Use one query to define another

steps.headline: A subquery is a query in brackets that supplies a value or a set to the outer query.

lead.text: The inner query runs first and passes its answer to the outer query. That answer can be a value or a set of ids.
EXISTS asks only whether the inner query returns any row at all.
The outer condition needs a number to compare with, and the subquery works it out first. One amount is unknown.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with the average the subquery found. An amount equal to it would not pass a strict comparison.

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strictly above 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: IN keeps a row when its value is in the set the subquery returns. The outer result still has one row per order.

reveal.text: You found the customers first and then their orders. An order with an unknown amount still counts: IN looks at the customer.

queries.label: North customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: South customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Which customers have at least one order?

workedSteps.text: Take one customer at a time.
Ask the inner query whether any order has customer_id = 1.
NOT EXISTS keeps the customer whose inner query finds nothing.

queries.label: At least one order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: A subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row is called correlated. Its answer can change from one outer row to the next.

queries.label: Above overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above its item average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lessons.orientation: Use scalar subqueries, IN and EXISTS without multiplying the outer result.
lessons.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

recap.keyIdea: A subquery supplies a value or a set to an outer query. EXISTS tests for a match without multiplying the outer rows.

recap.nextHook: Next, stack two results with UNION.

lessons.title: Combine reports deliberately

steps.headline: UNION stacks two results of the same shape, and UNION ALL keeps every row.

lead.text: UNION puts one query's rows under another's. Both queries must return the same number of columns.
UNION removes repeated rows from the stack. UNION ALL keeps them.
One query selects the ids of paid orders. Another selects the ids of orders worth at least 40. Think about what combining two results means.

reveal.text: You chose how the results are combined: stacked, not matched by a key. A join would attach columns instead.

queries.label: Paid orders
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Paid or at least 40
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Combine paid ids with at-least-40 ids, keeping repeats.

workedSteps.text: List the ids from each query.
UNION ALL keeps every occurrence, so an id in both lists appears twice.
UNION would collapse each repeated id into one row.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Keep occurrences
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION ALL SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: UNION removes repeated rows from the combined result.

reveal.text: You removed the ids that both queries returned. Plain UNION counts each different row once.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Keep occurrences
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION ALL SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: UNION compares whole rows. A column that differs makes two rows different, even when the id repeats.

reveal.text: You compared the id and the label together. A label turns a repeat into a new row.

queries.label: Id only
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and selection label
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'paid' AS selection FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id, 'large' AS selection FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id, selection;

lead.text: ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result. Remember that UNION has already removed repeats by then.

queries.label: Combined result
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First three combined ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

lessons.orientation: Stack compatible results with UNION or UNION ALL and account for overlapping rows.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Chess club has Ann, Bo, Cy and Di. Drama club has Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. The head wants one list of every pupil in either club.

intro.promise: By the end you'll stack two results, and say when repeated rows stay or collapse.

recap.keyIdea: UNION stacks results of the same shape and removes repeated rows. UNION ALL keeps every occurrence, and a differing column keeps rows apart.

lessons.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

steps.headline: A window function adds a value to each row and keeps every row.

lead.text: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. A window function does not: it adds a value beside each row.
OVER (ORDER BY ...) sets the order it uses. ROW_NUMBER numbers each row separately. RANK and DENSE_RANK give tied rows the same number.
One query groups the known amounts. The other adds a window calculation. Compare what each does to the rows.

reveal.text: You saw what the window version kept: the individual rows. The grouped version collapsed them into one row per amount.

queries.label: Query A
queries.sql: SELECT amount, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL GROUP BY amount ORDER BY amount DESC;

queries.label: Query B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

steps.headline: Rank the orders by customer_id with RANK.

workedSteps.text: Order the rows by customer_id.
Tied rows share a rank.
The next rank is one more than the number of rows before it.
workedSteps.math: order 103: two rows before, so rank 3

queries.label: Rank with RANK
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Number with ROW_NUMBER
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

lead.text: Order the amounts largest first. For RANK, count the rows that come before the amount you are asked about.

reveal.text: You counted the rows ahead and added one. Ties are part of that count, which is why RANK can leave gaps.

queries.label: Number each row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Share ranks for equal amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: DENSE_RANK also gives tied rows the same rank. It never skips: the next different amount takes the next integer.

reveal.text: You counted different amounts, not rows. Choose RANK or DENSE_RANK by what the report should mean.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: The window ranks by everything inside OVER (ORDER BY ...). Think about what a second column does to a tie.

queries.label: Rank the amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank amount and id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK and choose tie behaviour deliberately.
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four runners finish in 10, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. Runners with equal times share a place.

intro.promise: By the end you'll rank rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK or DENSE_RANK and say what happens to ties.

recap.keyIdea: A window function ranks rows without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER never ties. RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not.

blocks.text: You placed the 14-second runner 4th, then ranked the amount 40 as 3 with RANK and 2 with DENSE_RANK.

recap.nextHook: Next, restart the numbering inside each partition.

lessons.title: Choose which rows a window sees

steps.headline: PARTITION BY gives each group its own window, so calculations restart inside it.

lead.text: Without PARTITION BY, all rows share one window. PARTITION BY customer_id makes a separate window for each customer.
ROW_NUMBER restarts in each one. SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) puts the group total beside every row.
One query numbers all six orders in a single run. The other numbers each customer's orders separately.

reveal.text: You followed the numbering into one customer's window. It restarts where a new customer begins.

queries.label: One global window
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: One window per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Put each customer's total beside every one of their orders.

workedSteps.text: Split the rows into one window per customer.
Add the known amounts inside each window.
GROUP BY would give one row per customer instead.

queries.label: Customer totals beside orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Customer totals as groups
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS customer_total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: A window total is the sum over the partition. Every row of that partition shows the same value.

reveal.text: You added inside one partition. The total repeats beside each of its orders.

queries.label: Group the report
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Keep rows with status totals
queries.sql: SELECT id, status, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: NTILE(n) splits the ordered rows into n buckets as evenly as it can. Bucket sizes differ by at most one, and larger buckets come first.

reveal.text: You shared rows out by position. Buckets divide rows, not different amounts.

queries.label: Split A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Split B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A calculated position is a column of a result, not of the table. Think about where a filter can see it.

queries.label: Number all customer orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First order per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, position FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Calculate within each row's group and filter the resulting values.
lessons.reviewLabel: Choose which rows a window sees
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Class A pupils scored 6 and 8. Class B has one pupil, who scored 5. Beside every pupil you write their own class total.

intro.promise: By the end you'll restart a window calculation inside each group, and filter on its result.

recap.keyIdea: PARTITION BY gives each group its own window. Calculations restart inside it, and filtering on the result needs an outer query.

blocks.text: You wrote a class total of 14, then restarted numbering at 1 for customer 2. A paid total of 200 sat beside each paid order.

recap.nextHook: Next, add running totals and look at neighbouring rows.

lessons.title: Read the rows before and after

steps.headline: A frame says which rows count toward each row's value.

lead.text: A window can sum the rows from the first one up to the current one. That is a running total, and the frame is the range of rows it adds.
The order inside OVER decides which row is first, and so which rows come before.
The frame here runs from the first ordered row to the current row. The last amount is unknown, so it adds no known value.

reveal.text: You added the rows up to and including the current one. The grand total would use every row at once.

queries.label: Known grand total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Running known total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Add the amounts up by day, once with ROWS and once with RANGE.

workedSteps.text: ROWS adds records one at a time in the order given.
workedSteps.math: orders 102 then 103 on the same day: 100, then 180

workedSteps.text: RANGE adds every row that ties on the ordering value together.
The frame describes which rows contribute.

queries.label: ROWS frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: RANGE frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: LAG(amount) returns the amount from the previous row in the window order. The first row has no previous row.

reveal.text: You read one row back in the stated order. Reversing the order would change which row counts as previous.

queries.label: Previous in increasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Previous in decreasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: LEAD is the mirror of LAG. It reads the next row in the window order instead of the previous one.

queries.label: Next amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lessons.orientation: Specify running frames and use LAG or LEAD with an explicit ordering.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read the rows before and after
lessons.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bank statement lists deposits of 30, 10 and 50 pounds in order. Each line shows the balance so far.

recap.keyIdea: A frame decides which rows a window value adds, and LAG and LEAD read the neighbours in the stated order. A NULL there can mean no neighbour or no value.

blocks.text: You reached a balance of 90, then a running total of 180 at order 103. LAG gave 80 at order 104 and LEAD gave 40 at order 103.
